title: Rust HTTP execution and request boundaries
summary: Review HTTP request processing against the server's real runtime, state-sharing topology, input contracts, and failure semantics.

checks.question: Can work performed by this handler or middleware monopolize an executor worker or exhaust its blocking-work capacity under the expected concurrency?
checks.applicability: Synchronous database calls, filesystem access, compression, password hashing, model inference, blocking locks, and new task spawning.
valid_counterexamples: Short, bounded CPU work can be performed inline when it fits the request latency and scheduling budget.
A synchronous server or dedicated worker can intentionally perform blocking I/O.
A brief uncontended standard mutex critical section can be appropriate when it does not suspend or create a progress dependency.
evidence_needed: Actual runtime and worker configuration, plus whether called libraries block or yield.
Worst-case work duration, concurrent request count, and any work-pool admission bound.
Cancellation and timeout behavior for delegated work, including whether it continues after the request ends.
not_a_rule: An async function is not automatically nonblocking.
spawn_blocking does not provide unlimited capacity or cancel already running work when its caller times out.
HTTP services do not universally require an async architecture.

checks.question: Does application state have the ownership and synchronization required by the threads and tasks that actually access it, without exposing request-specific data to unrelated requests?
checks.applicability: Application state registration, worker factories, caches, sessions, lock scopes, global variables, and background tasks.
valid_counterexamples: Worker-local state on a supported single-threaded executor can use non-Send or non-Sync types when they never cross that boundary.
A thread-safe pool or immutable configuration object may be shared without another application-level lock.
Connection pools and caches can intentionally outlive individual requests.
evidence_needed: Framework trait bounds and where state is constructed, cloned, moved, or shared across workers.
Mutating access paths, lock ordering and scope, and whether guards span suspension points.
Isolation of per-user or per-request fields and lifecycle ownership for background work.
not_a_rule: All web state need not be Sync; requirements depend on its actual use and framework bounds.
Arc does not make its contents thread-safe.
Duplicating state per worker is not equivalent to sharing one authoritative mutable value.

checks.question: Before externally supplied data causes expensive work or state changes, are its size, business invariants, and caller permissions checked at the appropriate boundary?
checks.applicability: Routes, extractors, deserialization, upload handling, pagination, middleware order, and conversion of request types into domain commands.
valid_counterexamples: Validation already enforced by a trusted extractor or domain constructor need not be duplicated in each handler.
A streaming upload can be validated incrementally with explicit byte and time limits.
A public read-only route can intentionally require no authentication.
evidence_needed: Body, decompression, collection, and pagination limits before allocations or fan-out.
Which checks deserialization performs versus remaining semantic checks such as ranges and cross-field constraints.
Authentication/authorization placement relative to resource lookup and mutation, and rejection tests for invalid requests.
not_a_rule: Successfully parsing JSON does not establish business validity or authorization.
A typed identifier does not prove the caller may access the identified resource.
Not every route needs the same limits, middleware, or authentication policy.

checks.question: Do errors, timeouts, and client disconnects leave both the public response and any already-started effects consistent with the endpoint's documented contract?
checks.applicability: Error-to-response conversion, transaction boundaries, middleware timeouts, streaming responses, detached jobs, and request cancellation.
valid_counterexamples: A durable job endpoint can return acceptance while explicitly transferring completion ownership to a background worker.
A streaming response may need to report failure through its framing or terminate the stream after headers have been sent.
Safe user-facing validation details can be returned while internal dependency details remain private.
evidence_needed: Mappings for client errors, missing resources, conflicts, dependency failures, and internal failures.
Response-commit point, side-effect commit point, and state left when the future is dropped or a timeout fires.
Redacted diagnostics with correlation identifiers and tests that distinguish no effect, completed effect, and uncertain outcome.
not_a_rule: A timeout response does not prove that a database or remote side effect was rolled back.
Returning an error does not undo earlier mutations.
Request completion need not destroy explicitly owned background work or shared service resources.
